paper.title: What Stops Recursive Self-Improvement in Robotics? Lessons from 123 Rounds of Agentic Skill Discovery
paper.central_claim: In a 123-round run of an agentic robot self-improvement loop (GPT coding agents in Codex CLI proposing skill code or external models, accepted only after physical simulation tests, with humans allowed to repair only the testing harness), the agent can discover missing capabilities (e.g. active viewing) but its accepted changes did not add up: the target RoboCasa Fridge task never succeeded. The agent was rarely the bottleneck; three surrounding factors were: (1) chained perception modules do not represent relations so the agent displaces semantics into ever-growing geometric code, (2) skill chains lock learning onto the first failing step, (3) the harness (evaluators, gates, memory, embodiment description) decides what is learned.
paper.claim_scope_note: Negative-result / diagnostic report of one long run: one simulator (RoboCasa), one kitchen layout, three tasks, no independent replicates or ablations (authors' own limitation); recommendations D1-D12 are untested hypotheses.

gap.author_gap: Coding agents improve software in loops (Voyager, Eureka, DGM) and the idea has reached robots (RHO, ASPIRE, ENPIRE), yet it is unclear whether improvements accumulate on long household tasks, and if not, what stops them and whether a stronger agent would fix it.
gap.checked_gap: Specific and important: the closest robot systems report gains on benchmarks (ASPIRE LIBERO-Pro/Robosuite/BEHAVIOR-1K, ENPIRE real-world), while no long fully-recorded failing run is given; the paper explains these systems' success via the three conditions they satisfy by construction. Neighbour texts were not pinned or rerun, so the cross-system explanation is the authors' reading.
gap.lineage: Voyager / Eureka / Reflexion / Darwin Godel Machine -> RHO / ASPIRE / ENPIRE (robot self-improvement with gains) -> this long-run diagnostic with a three-condition account

matches.tactic_steps_checked: The audited assumption is that software-style self-improvement carries over (failures are representable, fixes expressible, tests resolvable); the run constructs the violation in a long robot loop and characterises where each condition breaks before offering recommendations (failure-case characterisation precedes the proposals, as the card's success conditions favour). There is no relaxation with a re-proved guarantee; the pivot is a diagnostic framework and untested design hypotheses.
matches.success_failure_checks: Success: prior approach shown to fail precisely at the audited assumption (met by Table 2 mapping), new/weakened conditions characterised (partial), systematic design template rather than one-off (partial: D1-D12). Failure: validation against an adaptive/informed setting (absent: single run), stacking without isolating which pivot is load-bearing (partly: three lessons not isolated from each other), differentiation from near-identical precedent (present in Sec 9).
matches.reason: A negative-result paper whose operation is auditing and violating the 'software-style loop' assumption; main card chosen because no other of the 15 mains describes a failure-mode audit of a method class. All six sub-cards under this parent (C01, C05, C11, C19, C28, C29) concern security loci, identifiability, selection rules, statistical certificates, distributed optimisation or convergence assumptions, so sub_id is null. controlled_diagnostic_design was read and rejected as no controlled instrument is built (the authors state the study is not controlled).

rs_pattern.reason: One partial-fit main card; supporting empty because no distinct second operation is executed.
rs_pattern.resolves_problem: No: the problem (making robot self-improvement compound) is diagnosed, not solved; the recommended fixes are untested.

domain_pattern.unassigned: Evaluator capture, semantic displacement and frontier lock are paper-specific diagnoses with no card; a candidate card would need a second independent full-text paper.
revision_proposals: Add to K401 'When it fails': evaluator/embodiment-description errors exploited by the proposer, noisy and coarse gates, fixed-seed evidence fixed points, lost requests (needs a second paper for a candidate-level change).

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: K401's trace-driven harness revision loop is the object whose underlying assumptions the paper audits; the audit shows where K401-style loops break (evaluators, gates, memory).
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions_and_differences: K401 assumes a search set separate from test and an optimizer barred from hidden state; here these were violated early and repaired, and the revised object is robot skill code rather than a harness around a frozen agent.

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: Decomposing outcomes by first-failed step and per-seed patterns operationalises the audit.
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions_and_differences: K804 expects repeated runs with endpoints; here repeats are deterministic replays of four seeds.

claims.text: Accepted improvements did not add up: the target task never succeeded.
claims.setting: RoboCasa Fridge/Cabinet/Sink, 123 rounds, four fixed seeds per task
claims.selection_vs_test: dev tasks are also the reported tasks; gates use fresh scenes and a held-out task
claims.result_denominator: Fridge 0/486, Cabinet 0/256, Sink 14/230 (9 with failed intermediate steps)
claims.counterevidence: Effective independent scenes per task is four; one run
claims.allowed_conclusion: In this run on these tasks and seeds, accepted changes did not produce task-level success.

claims.text: The agent can discover a missing capability (active viewing) from failures alone.
claims.result_denominator: one capability; model used 520 calls in 295 rollouts
claims.counterevidence: Evaluator repair by humans preceded discovery; target-not-in-view still appears later in Tables 4 and 8
claims.allowed_conclusion: Qualitative existence proof of an agent-requested, deployed active-search model, after human evaluator repair; its effect on failure rates is not quantified.

claims.text: Chained perception modules do not represent relations and the code-writing agent displaces semantics into geometry (Lesson 1).
claims.baseline_control: none; a VLM probe on 4 recorded views
claims.result_denominator: region skill 3,056 lines / 33 thresholds; 27 attempts rescued seed 69 always and 68 never; wrong_region in all 62 late rollouts of three seeds; VLM 4/4
claims.counterevidence: No benchmark of SAM 3 / Florence-2 on relations; VLM check is feasibility on four frames
claims.allowed_conclusion: Descriptive account of one failing front; generality of 'modules cannot represent relations' untested.

claims.text: Skill chains lock learning onto the first step (Lesson 2).
claims.baseline_control: analytic model Delta S = pi_j Delta p_j prod p_i
claims.result_denominator: 57% fail step 1; 2.7% pass four steps; 0.9% pass five; round-118 grasp win followed by 0/60 successes
claims.counterevidence: Same run, no interventions to relieve the lock
claims.allowed_conclusion: Well supported as an explanation of why local wins did not reach the task in this run.

claims.text: The harness decides what the agent learns (Lesson 3).
claims.result_denominator: 276 boundary successes; 119 rejected candidates with a rescue; 16 of 36 re-runs not reproducing; 88 lost requests; 11 unused models; 113 human repairs
claims.counterevidence: Repairs, model swaps and providers changed along the same timeline; framing effect is uncontrolled
claims.allowed_conclusion: Strong descriptive evidence that harness errors shaped what was learned; effect sizes unattributed.

claims.text: The agent was rarely the bottleneck.
claims.result_denominator: no manipulation of agent, compute or representation
claims.counterevidence: Authors state they cannot say whether a different agent, compute or representation would solve it

claims.text: Design implications D1-D12 restore the three conditions.

assessment.evidence_level_reason: Closed-loop RoboCasa simulation with native task success and complete per-task denominators; one simulator, four fixed seeds per task, development and reported tasks overlap, no transfer evidence (and no positive transfer claim).
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: In one 123-round run of a GPT-agent-driven robot self-improvement loop on RoboCasa kitchen tasks, 57 accepted skill changes and 86 model registrations yielded no success on the target Fridge task (0/486) and only mostly accidental Sink successes, and the recorded failures trace to relational perception, chain-length frontier lock, and evaluator/gate/memory defects that humans repaired 113 times; whether a different agent or budget would change this, and whether the proposed fixes work, are untested.
unresolved: Effect of a different agent, compute or representation
Generality beyond one layout and three tasks
Quantitative evidence on SAM 3 / Florence-2 relation failures
Reconciling 'out-of-view failures disappeared' with later target_not_in_view rows
assessment.reproduction_note: All results are author-reported; nothing was run by us.

G.reason: A specific, important question (do agent-made robot improvements compound, and what stops them) located against named neighbours (Voyager, Eureka, DGM, RHO, ASPIRE, ENPIRE) whose reported gains are explained by conditions they satisfy by construction; the remaining gap (controlled tests, other agents and setups) is explicitly bounded in Sec 10.

M.reason: A simple chain model (S = prod p_j, Delta S formula) and a three-condition account (representability, expressibility, resolvability) that map each failure to a mechanism and give distinguishable predictions with falsifying experiments (Table 3); the framework is deliberately diagnostic and the explanations rest on one run, so not 4.

X.reason: The loop (roles, information each agent sees, models and effort per round, time caps, gate sequence, persistence, human-repair rule) is described in detail with a round-by-round record, measurement tables and model-use table, and failure boundaries and limitations are explicit; prompts and code are not shown, which stops short of reproducibility but not of reconstructability.

measurement.reason: Native environment success with complete per-task counts and an audit of the evaluator (found and repaired capture, accidental successes separated), which strongly supports the negative outcome; held back by privileged step evaluators that were buggy for much of the run, effective n of four seeds per task, and an unquantified 'out-of-view failures disappeared' claim that Tables 4/8 partly contradict.

causality.reason: Mechanisms are dissected with counts, but harness repairs, model versions and providers changed together, no agent/compute/representation was varied, and the central 'agent was rarely the bottleneck' is not interventionally tested (authors concede); the prompt-paragraph and effort observations are uncontrolled before/after.

holdout.reason: Reported tasks are the development tasks on four fixed seeds with no task-level gain (anchor v2: overlap with gain approx 0); a held-out task and fresh scenes exist for gating but were visible to agents before round 74; scope is one simulator and layout, honestly stated.

statistics.reason: Failure denominators are exceptionally complete (first-failed-step distribution, per-seed endpoints, accepted/rejected counts, reproduction of 36 re-run pairs), but there is a single loop run with no replicates or intervals and four reused deterministic seeds.

cost.reason: Time per round (1-3 h), several weeks of operation, 847 attempts with per-attempt caps, agent model/effort schedule and 113 human repairs are disclosed; no token or dollar totals, and no budget-matched alternative.

status.reason: Complete HTML full text with all appendices read; scoped as a negative-result/diagnostic report evaluated against its own central claims.
